subject: phy
title: Superposition
subtitle: Interference, stationary waves and diffraction patterns.
concept: The principle of superposition states that when waves overlap, the resultant displacement equals the algebraic sum of individual displacements.
Constructive interference occurs when waves are in phase; destructive when they are antiphase (π out of phase).
Stationary (standing) waves form when two identical waves travel in opposite directions; they have nodes and antinodes.

notes.heading: Principle of Superposition and Interference
items: When two or more waves overlap, the resultant displacement at any point and time is the algebraic sum of the individual displacements. This is the principle of superposition.

Constructive interference occurs where waves arrive in phase (path difference = nλ, n = 0, 1, 2…) — amplitudes add. Destructive interference occurs where they arrive in antiphase (path difference = (n + ½)λ) — amplitudes subtract.
Stable interference requires coherent sources — sources with the same frequency and a constant phase difference. Two separate lamps are not coherent.

notes.heading: Young's Double-Slit Experiment
items: A single light source illuminates two narrow slits, creating two coherent secondary sources. The slits diffract the light, which then interferes. Bright fringes (maxima) appear where the path difference from the two slits is nλ; dark fringes (minima) where it is (n + ½)λ.
Fringe spacing: Δy = λD/d, where λ is the wavelength, D is the slit-to-screen distance, and d is the slit separation. Reducing d or increasing D gives wider, more widely spaced fringes.

notes.heading: Stationary Waves
items: Stationary (standing) waves form when two waves of equal frequency and amplitude travel in opposite directions. The superposition produces points of zero amplitude (nodes, separated by λ/2) and points of maximum amplitude (antinodes, midway between nodes).
Unlike progressive waves, stationary waves do not transfer energy along the medium. All points between two nodes oscillate in phase; points on opposite sides of a node are in antiphase.
Fundamental mode (first harmonic) of a string fixed at both ends: the string length = λ/2, so f₁ = v/(2L). The nth harmonic has frequency n×f₁.

notes.heading: Diffraction Grating
items: The grating equation: d sin θ = nλ, where d = slit spacing (1/N lines per metre), θ = angle of the nth order maximum, n = order number. A grating with more lines per mm has smaller d and produces more widely spaced maxima.
The maximum order nₘₐₓ occurs when sin θ = 1 (θ = 90°): nₘₐₓ = d/λ. Gratings produce sharp, bright maxima — useful for precise wavelength measurement in spectroscopy.

definitions.body: When two or more waves overlap, the resultant displacement at any point is the algebraic sum of the individual displacements.
Sources with the same frequency and a constant (not necessarily zero) phase difference; required for stable interference patterns.
A point on a stationary wave where the amplitude is always zero; located at positions of permanent destructive interference.
A point on a stationary wave with maximum amplitude; located midway between adjacent nodes.
Distance between adjacent bright (or dark) fringes in a double-slit experiment: Δy = λD/d.

workedExamples.q: In Young's double-slit experiment, λ = 590 nm, d = 0.50 mm, D = 2.0 m. Find the fringe spacing.
A string of length 0.60 m vibrates in its fundamental mode. Waves travel at 240 m s⁻¹. Find the frequency.

mistakes: Confusing path difference (physical) with phase difference — path difference of λ = phase difference of 2π (360°).
Forgetting that adjacent nodes are λ/2 apart (not λ).
Using the wrong formula for closed vs open pipe harmonics.
tips: Coherence is essential for stable fringes — two separate lamps don't interfere because they aren't coherent.
Grating: more orders are observable at smaller λ or larger d. Check sinθ ≤ 1 for maximum order.
Stationary waves don't transfer energy; progressive (travelling) waves do.

flashcards.q: State the conditions for constructive and destructive interference.
flashcards.a: Constructive: path difference = nλ (in phase). Destructive: path difference = (n+½)λ (antiphase).

flashcards.q: What is the fringe spacing formula in Young's double-slit experiment?
flashcards.a: Δy = λD/d (wavelength × screen distance / slit separation).

flashcards.q: What is the distance between adjacent nodes in a stationary wave?

flashcards.a: d sinθ = nλ (d = slit spacing, θ = angle of nth order maximum).
Sources with the same frequency and a constant phase difference — needed for stable interference.

flashcards.q: What is the fundamental frequency of a string of length L with wave speed v?
flashcards.a: f₁ = v/(2L) (one half-wavelength fits along the string).

questions.q: Two waves are in antiphase. What type of interference results?
questions.exp: Antiphase (180° or π phase difference, path difference = λ/2) → destructive interference → minimum amplitude.

questions.q: In Young's double-slit: λ is doubled, d is halved. What happens to fringe spacing?
questions.exp: Δy = λD/d; if λ→2λ and d→d/2: Δy = (2λ)D/(d/2) = 4λD/d → quadrupled.

questions.q: Adjacent nodes in a stationary wave are 0.15 m apart. What is the wavelength?
A diffraction grating has d = 2×10⁻⁶ m. For λ = 500 nm, what is the maximum diffraction order?
What type of sources are needed for a stable interference pattern?
questions.exp: Coherent sources (same frequency, constant phase difference) are required for a stable, observable interference pattern.

recall: Explain the conditions for constructive and destructive interference.
Derive and apply the fringe spacing formula.
Describe the formation of stationary waves and identify nodes and antinodes.
